# Compounding Pressures and Scaling Limits {#sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales}

::: {.epigraph}
> "[F]eedback is a method of controlling a system by reinserting into it the results of its past performance. If these results are merely used as numerical data for the criticism of the system and its regulation, we have the simple feedback of the control engineers."
>
> — Norbert Wiener, *The Human Use of Human Beings*, revised edition [@Wiener1989HumanUse, p. 61]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Why has system and chip design become harder to carry through, and where might AI assistance be useful?*

**Core thesis:** *Compounding pressures across physical scaling, specialization, software co-evolution, and verification demand new abstractions, but assistance helps only when it targets the work that actually limits the next design decision.*
:::

System and chip design increasingly depends on choices that must be evaluated together. Device scaling still improves transistor density, but no longer supplies the same broadly reusable gains in frequency and energy efficiency. Specialization, local data reuse, and new packaging can recover performance, while binding the result more tightly to software and physical implementation. Each promising architectural change can therefore require work in several disciplines before its value is known.

Establishing the system value of these changes requires executable software, representative workloads, and physical and functional checks. Comparing candidates draws on finite simulation, verification, and review capacity, so the cost of learning whether a change helps can become the limiting pressure. The resulting bottleneck differs across projects (@fig-ch02-cover-map). Point AI assistance, an AI-native design system (both defined in @sec-moonshot), or conventional automation can improve the study when it addresses that bottleneck and its gains justify the total cost. Complexity alone does not establish a need for AI.

![**Compounding pressures shift the architectural bottleneck.** Fading automatic technology gains, coupled design obligations across hardware and software, and finite simulation and verification capacity converge to limit design velocity. AI assistance helps most when it targets the specific engineering work delaying the next supported decision.](images/ch02-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch02-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which fading technology gains, coupled design obligations, and finite checking capacity converge on the work limiting the next supported decision."}

A team waiting for a compiler path faces a different problem from one waiting for simulations or expert review. The pressures traced in this chapter explain why such delays arise, but only measurements from the project can show which work must improve.

## Where Engineering Time Goes in Modern Chip Design

The cost of architectural exploration is visible in a familiar design choice. When an architect considers expanding an on-chip level-2 (L2) cache to relieve memory bandwidth pressure, a capacity-focused simulation may favor the larger cache because it reduces misses. In silicon, however, the additional static random-access memory (SRAM) bitcells consume die area, lengthen interconnects,[^fn-rc-delay-c02] and increase leakage current. Within the thermal envelope of a passively cooled mobile device, that extra leakage reduces the power budget left for the compute cores. A simulated drop in cache misses therefore answers only part of the architectural question.

[^fn-rc-delay-c02]: **Interconnect resistance and capacitance**: A wire has electrical resistance, while neighboring conductors contribute capacitance. Charging that capacitance through the resistance takes time. Narrower wires increase resistance, and long connections add both resistance and capacitance, so a larger storage structure can take longer to access even when its transistors switch quickly.

Software offers another way to attack the same memory bottleneck. Loop tiling can reduce the working set that must remain on chip at one time, allowing a smaller cache or buffer to retain useful data, although the tiled loops can add control overhead. If the schedule uses direct memory access (DMA) to feed an explicitly managed local buffer or scratchpad, it also incurs transfer-descriptor and coordination costs. To weigh a larger L2 cache against a tiled software schedule, the architect needs both an executable schedule and characterized physical memory macros. Beyond building those inputs, the architect has to decide which hardware–software pairs are worth testing and which measurements will separate them.

Weighing hardware against software in this way cuts across the boundaries that earlier abstractions were built to separate. Each jump in abstraction kept implementation complexity manageable by hiding lower-level detail behind automated tools. Register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions let engineers specify synchronous circuit behavior without placing individual gates by hand.[^fn-rtl-c02] Logic synthesis and place-and-route tools then generated the gate-level layout. As @sec-moonshot showed, those abstractions succeeded because trustworthy verification tools, such as equivalence checkers and timing analyzers, checked the lower-level implementation automatically. Today's cross-layer, specialized architectures strain that model because hardware and software choices interact across the boundary, forcing many more coupled candidates through slow implementation tools and the timing and power signoff checks that precede fabrication.

[^fn-rtl-c02]: **RTL as an architectural contract**: RTL specifies synchronous state updates and transfers between registers. Changing pipeline stages or interface timing can require restructuring these transfers, so an architectural alternative may need more implementation work than changing a parameter.

A *design path* is a sequence of work that proposes an architectural change, builds candidate artifacts, runs the relevant tools, and compares the results. In the cache study, one path evaluates two L2 capacities under a representative workload. It becomes a closed *design loop* only when returned evidence changes the represented design state and triggers another allowed action. High leakage might lead the architect to record the smaller cache in the design state and take the next allowed action, evaluating a tiled schedule. A fixed parameter sweep collects measurements across a preset grid; a design loop uses the results to determine subsequent work. This closing condition distinguishes a loop from a sequence of successful tool runs.

Every turn of that loop spends engineering time, electronic design automation (EDA) tool licenses, and human review on inputs that span RTL source, execution traces, timing constraints, and specifications of which blocks may power down. The breakdown of classical transistor and wire scaling explains why more architectural choices now require such cross-layer experiments.

## The End of Free Scaling and the Push Toward Specialization {#sec-fracturing-technology-dividend}

For roughly thirty years, processor performance advanced under classical Dennard scaling, in which each process generation delivered smaller, faster transistors at constant power density (@tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison) [@Moore1965Cramming; @DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Today, device technology still supplies transistor density, but it no longer delivers proportional gains in frequency, single-thread performance, or energy efficiency. To extract more performance, architects now have to make choices that tightly bind microarchitecture, software mapping, and physical implementation together.

### The Collapse of Dennard Scaling and the Shift to Specialization

Classical Dennard scaling balanced denser transistors against lower power per transistor. Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ reduced area by $1/\kappa^2$, while lower capacitance and supply voltage reduced switching energy enough to permit a higher clock frequency at constant dynamic power density [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. The dynamic-power relation $P_{\mathrm{dyn}} = \alpha C V_{dd}^{2} f$ makes voltage's role explicit: its contribution is squared, alongside switching activity $\alpha$, capacitance $C$, and frequency $f$.

The classical balance broke down in the mid-2000s because supply voltage could no longer fall alongside feature size. Lower voltage slows transistor switching unless the threshold voltage also drops, but lowering that threshold increases off-state leakage.[^fn-subthreshold-leakage-c02] Device physics thus forces a trade-off among switching speed, active power, and leakage. Once voltage reductions stalled, process shrinks alone could no longer deliver simultaneous gains in clock frequency and energy efficiency [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach].

[^fn-subthreshold-leakage-c02]: **Subthreshold leakage**: Below its threshold voltage, a transistor's current falls exponentially with gate voltage, at best by a factor of ten for every 60\ mV at room temperature. Lowering the threshold by 60\ mV can therefore raise off-state leakage by up to about ten times, which is why supply voltage stopped falling with each process generation.

The comparison in @tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison isolates what changes when voltage and frequency stop scaling. Its simplified post-Dennard case holds activity, voltage, and frequency fixed while retaining idealized area and gate-capacitance scaling. Leakage and interconnect capacitance are excluded from that calculation, although a real implementation must account for both.

| Device Parameter | Classical Dennard Scaling ($\kappa > 1$) | Simplified Post-Dennard Case | Limiting Physical Constraint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transistor Area ($W \times L$)** | $1/\kappa^2$ | $1/\kappa^2$ | Gate pitch scaling continues |
| **Supply Voltage ($V_{dd}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Leakage and switching-speed trade-off |
| **Gate Capacitance ($C_{\text{gate}}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1/\kappa$ *(idealized)* | Gate and interconnect capacitance scale differently |
| **Operating Frequency ($f$)** | $\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Thermal dissipation and leakage limit frequency gains |
| **Dynamic Power Density ($P_{\mathrm{dyn}} / A$)** | $1$ *(constant)* | $\kappa$ *(under stated assumptions)* | Dark silicon and thermal limits |
: **Classical Dennard scaling versus a simplified post-Dennard case.** Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ historically kept dynamic power density constant while increasing operating frequency. With voltage, frequency, and activity held fixed in the displayed post-Dennard case, dynamic power density rises by $\kappa$; leakage, interconnect, and nonideal geometric scaling make real product behavior implementation-dependent. {#tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison tbl-colwidths="[24,24,28,24]"}

Under the table's post-Dennard assumptions, power per transistor falls more slowly than transistor density rises. More transistors can therefore fit in the same area without all being able to switch at once within the same power budget. Leakage and interconnect costs further affect the usable fraction in a physical chip.

@fig-microprocessor-trends maps this architectural evolution across three eras. It joins fifty years of microprocessor scaling data from Karl Rupp's CPU sample (1971–2021) [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData] with a 2012–2026 frontier compiled from the published specifications of twenty-five accelerators, including GPUs [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @JouppiEtAl2021TenLessons; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @AMD2025CDNA3; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2013K20XBoardSpec; @AMD2021CDNA2; @Myrhang2023AMDInstinctHPC; @Intel2023Gaudi2Datasheet; @Intel2024Gaudi3Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet; @NVIDIA2025BlackwellUltraBlog; @NVIDIA2026RubinBlog; @Cerebras2019WSE; @Cerebras2021WSE2; @Cerebras2024WSE3]. In the *device-scaling era* (1971–2005), single-thread performance, clock frequency, and transistor counts all climbed by orders of magnitude, though at different rates. Around the 2005 Dennard boundary, clock frequency stalled near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$ in this sample. Single-thread performance growth fell from about 52% per year (1986–2003) to about 23% per year, and to single digits by the late 2010s [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. This slowdown ushered in the *parallelism era* (2005–2016), as architects turned to multicore integration and sampled hardware thread counts climbed to 96 by 2016 and 128 by 2020. A third inflection around 2016 marks the *specialization era*, as dedicated datapaths became an increasingly important use of growing transistor budgets.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The readable stacked plot was deferred several pages under top-only placement. -->
![**Frequency scaling slows as transistor budgets and accelerator power ratings grow.** Four-year maxima from Rupp's CPU sample (1971–2021) [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData] join running maxima from twenty-five accelerators (2012–2026). Accelerator counts reach 336 billion transistors (4 trillion for wafer-scale parts), and power ratings reach $1{,}400\ \text{W}$. Ratings mix thermal design power, board-power limits, and total graphics power, not measured workload power. The CPU series establishes no later power ceiling. Accelerator sources and six dated design reports appear in the text; the hatched band after 2026 marks the emerging AI-native design frontier rather than a fourth measured trend.](images/fig-microprocessor-trends){#fig-microprocessor-trends width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Log-scale chart with CPU sample maxima ending in 2021 and accelerator specification frontiers extending to 2026. CPU frequency growth slows after 2005, while transistor counts and accelerator power ratings increase. A hatched band after 2026 marks a hypothesized AI-native design era; a separate rail dates six AI-assisted design reports."}

The divergence of these curves after 2005 [@Sutter2005FreeLunch] reflects the *dark silicon* limit [@EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon].[^fn-dark-silicon-c02] Once supply voltage stopped scaling, thermal budgets capped the fraction of a chip's transistors that could switch simultaneously at full clock frequency. Duplicating general-purpose cores during the parallelism era converted extra transistors into thread-level concurrency, but serial code sections and shared-memory traffic soon limited the return on adding more homogeneous cores.

Specialization answers that limit by spending the transistor and power budget on dedicated datapaths. Packaged accelerator transistor counts climb from 15.3 billion in the NVIDIA Tesla P100 (2016) to 208 billion in the dual-die Blackwell B200 (2024) and 336 billion in NVIDIA's Rubin GPU (2026) [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2026RubinBlog]. Cerebras goes further, integrating 4 trillion transistors on a single wafer-scale die [@Cerebras2024WSE3]. Over the same span, published accelerator power ratings rise from the P100's $300\ \text{W}$ thermal design power (TDP) to as much as $1{,}400\ \text{W}$ total graphics power in the Blackwell Ultra generation (2025) [@NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @NVIDIA2025BlackwellUltraBlog]. These ratings describe nominal hardware envelopes rather than measured application efficiency. Even so, they show why the industry has directed its silicon budget into regular matrix and tensor arrays. Such arrays amortize instruction fetch and decode across hundreds of arithmetic units, trading clock-rate scaling for dense spatial parallelism and local data reuse.

The hatched band in @fig-microprocessor-trends identifies the design process as a possible next source of improvement, rather than a measured successor to specialization. The dated reports alongside it document early applications to placement, design support, circuits, and generated processors or accelerators [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @Verkor2026DesignConductor; @Verkor2026DesignConductor2; @DeepMind2026AlphaEvolveImpact; @OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults]. They do not establish that an AI-native design system reduces total project cost against a comparably equipped conventional team. The pressure that motivates such a comparison begins with the physical and coordination costs of exploiting larger transistor budgets.

[^fn-dark-silicon-c02]: **Dark silicon**: Silicon that cannot all operate concurrently at full performance within the available power and thermal budget. Power gating, clock gating, and reduced operating rates are among the ways a design manages that limit.

### Diminishing Returns Inside General-Purpose Cores

General-purpose processors continue to improve through branch prediction, speculative execution, wider issue, and better memory hierarchies. These mechanisms can expose and exploit more instruction-level parallelism, but each one adds hardware that tracks and orders the extra work in flight.

The out-of-order issue window illustrates that cost. More entries let a core look farther ahead for independent instructions, while wider issue allows more instructions to execute per cycle. Completing instructions must broadcast result tags to waiting entries, however, and selection logic must choose which ready instructions proceed. Enlarging the window increases the load on those broadcast wires; widening issue adds comparison, arbitration, and bypass paths. Circuit analysis shows how wakeup, selection, and bypass delays limit the return on wider issue [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective], while wire delay restricts how far a signal can travel in a clock cycle [@AgarwalEtAl2000ClockRateVersusIPC].

Replicating cores does not escape this cost; it moves it into coherence, synchronization, and workload partitioning. General-purpose architectures continue to advance, but each gain in parallelism, whether inside one core or across many, has to pay for the structures that coordinate it.

### The Shift to Domain-Specific Accelerators

When a workload performs regular, predictable calculations, a specialized datapath can strip away most of that per-instruction coordination hardware and devote the silicon to dense arithmetic arrays. The trade works only if the memory system can keep those units fed.

The trade has produced a diverse population of accelerators rather than one canonical template, a shift the Project Brainwave team characterized as rapid architectural diversification [@ChungEtAl2018Brainwave]. Publicly announced AI chips, cards, and systems spread across the power–performance plane from milliwatt edge devices to multi-kilowatt data-center platforms (@fig-accelerator-landscape) [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS].

```{python}
#| label: fig-accelerator-landscape
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **AI accelerators span seven orders of magnitude in peak power.** Each point represents a
#|   publicly announced accelerator entry from the MIT Lincoln Laboratory survey, plotted as peak performance against
#|   peak power on log-log axes; the 180 entries across 170 accelerators span about $1\ \text{mW}$ to $23\ \text{kW}$ and
#|   $6\ \text{GOps/s}$ to $3.5 \times 10^7\ \text{GOps/s}$ [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS]. Marker shape and color denote form factor (circle chip, square card, triangle system), filled versus hollow markers
#|   distinguish training from inference parts, and dashed diagonals trace constant energy-efficiency contours
#|   from $100\ \text{GOps/W}\text{ to }100\ \text{TOPS/W}$. The resulting design space forms a dense, heterogeneous cloud
#|   rather than clustering around a single operating point.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-log scatter plot of about 180 AI accelerators, peak performance in giga-operations per second versus peak power in watts. Points span from subwatt embedded chips at the lower left to multi-kilowatt data-center systems at the upper right, roughly seven orders of magnitude in power and six in performance. Dashed diagonal lines mark constant energy efficiency from 100 giga-ops per watt to 100 tera-ops per watt. Chips are circles, cards squares, and systems triangles; training parts are filled and inference parts hollow."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
from _python.labels import place_labels

apply_style()

# Data: MIT Lincoln Laboratory AI accelerator survey, 2025 edition
# [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS], one row per publicly announced accelerator with a
# stated peak performance and power. Values are dataset-transcribed.
# Accessed 2026-07-19. Source data: data/datasets/chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
rows = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for d in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        try:
            perf = float(d["peak_performance_ops_per_s"]) / 1e9
            power = float(d["power_w"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        rows.append({"label": d["label"], "perf": perf, "power": power,
                     "form": d["form_factor"], "iort": d["inference_or_training"]})

forms = {"Chip": COLORS["workload"], "Card": COLORS["methods"], "System": COLORS["evidence"]}
markers = {"Chip": "o", "Card": "s", "System": "^"}  # shape as well as hue
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
xline = np.array([1e-3, 1e5])
for eff, lab in [(1e2, "100 GOPS/W"), (1e3, "1 TOPS/W"), (1e4, "10 TOPS/W"), (1e5, "100 TOPS/W")]:
    ax.plot(xline, eff * xline, ls=(0, (5, 4)), color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    x_pos = max(2.4e-3, 10.0 / eff)
    ax.text(x_pos, eff * x_pos * 1.3, lab, fontsize=4.6, color=COLORS["muted"],
            rotation=34, rotation_mode="anchor", va="bottom", ha="left", zorder=1)
for form, color in forms.items():
    for iort, filled in [("training", True), ("inference", False)]:
        pts = [d for d in rows if d["form"] == form and d["iort"] == iort]
        if not pts:
            continue
        xs = [d["power"] for d in pts]
        ys = [d["perf"] for d in pts]
        if filled:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolors="white", edgecolors=color, linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.95, zorder=3)
for txt, x, y in [("Very low power", 0.02, 3.0e3), ("Embedded / autonomous", 3.0, 1.2e1),
                  ("Data-center cards", 5e1, 2.5e6), ("Data-center systems", 1.5e4, 2.5e5)]:
    ax.text(x, y, txt, fontsize=5.2, fontstyle="italic", color=COLORS["muted"], ha="center", va="center", zorder=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(8e-4, 7e4)
ax.set_ylim(3, 1e8)
ax.set_xlabel("Peak power (W)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Peak performance (GOps/sec)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker=markers[f], ls="", markerfacecolor=c, markeredgecolor=c, markersize=5, label=f) for f, c in forms.items()]
handles += [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=COLORS["ink"], markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Training"),
            Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Inference")]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3, borderaxespad=0.4)
curated = ["Maxim", "GAP9", "Jetson1", "Perceive", "A100", "TPU4", "H100",
           "AMD-MI300X", "B200", "Gaudi3", "CS-2", "DGX-H100", "GroqNode", "Tachyum"]
by_label: dict[str, dict] = {}
for d in rows:
    if d["label"] not in by_label or d["perf"] > by_label[d["label"]]["perf"]:
        by_label[d["label"]] = d
items = [(by_label[n]["power"], by_label[n]["perf"], n) for n in curated if n in by_label]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.095, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)
```

The spread reflects deployment targets rather than a single ranking of designs, because the plotted points mix numerical precisions, supported operations, and chip, card, and system boundaries. A subwatt sensor processor emphasizes local storage and low-precision arithmetic to avoid costly off-chip transfers, whereas a data-center accelerator devotes orders of magnitude more power to compute arrays and high-bandwidth memory. The data-center end of that plane shows most clearly what happens when arithmetic grows faster than the memory that feeds it.

Across five NVIDIA GPU generations from Pascal P100 (2016) to Blackwell B200 (2024), peak dense half-precision floating-point (FP16) throughput grew by $106\times$ ($21.2\text{ to }2{,}250\ \text{TFLOPS}$). Off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) supply grew only $10.9\times$ ($732\text{ to }8{,}000\ \text{GB/s}$), roughly an order of magnitude less, while TDP rose $3.3\times$ ($300\text{ to }1{,}000\ \text{W}$) (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier a). With precision held fixed and excluding structured sparsity,[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02] this divergence reflects an architectural pivot from P100's conventional vector units to dedicated matrix Tensor Cores across successive process nodes and dual-reticle packaging [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief].

[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02]: **Structured sparsity**: Sparse matrices contain zero values whose arithmetic can sometimes be skipped. Hardware-supported structured sparsity limits the patterns of nonzero values so that dedicated hardware can process the remaining values efficiently. Advertised sparse throughput assumes those patterns; the comparison here uses dense throughput throughout.

Because arithmetic capacity expanded far faster than off-chip memory bandwidth, feeding these datapaths demands much higher data reuse inside the package. If we define a workload's *operational intensity* as the arithmetic operations executed per byte transferred across the HBM boundary, dividing peak compute rate by memory bandwidth gives the off-chip balance point plotted in @fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier b [@Williams2009Roofline]. That dense FP16 balance point rises tenfold, from $29\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on P100 to $295\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on H100, then plateaus at $281\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on B200 because eight-stack HBM3e bandwidth ($8\ \text{TB/s}$) keeps pace with the $2.3\times$ step in dense FP16 compute. B200's narrower 8-bit and 4-bit floating-point (FP8 and FP4) Tensor Core modes push the required reuse another $2\times\text{ to }4\times$ higher. A kernel operating below its target precision's balance point cannot saturate the matrix engines even with zero control stalls. Greater on-chip data reuse raises the kernel's operational intensity by reducing HBM traffic, whereas more HBM bandwidth lowers the hardware's balance point at a fixed peak compute rate.

![**Arithmetic scaling outpaces off-chip memory bandwidth.** (a) Growth relative to P100 in dense FP16 peak throughput, HBM bandwidth, and TDP across five GPU generations from P100 to B200 (2016–2024). (b) The dense FP16 off-chip balance point rises from 29\ FLOP/byte on P100 to 295\ FLOP/byte on H100 and 281\ FLOP/byte on B200, demanding steep operational intensity to saturate peak arithmetic. Hardware specifications exclude structured sparsity [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet].](images/fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier){#fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel chart for P100, V100, A100, H100, and B200 GPUs from 2016 to 2024. First panel shows dense FP16 peak throughput growing 106 times relative to P100 while HBM bandwidth grows 10.9 times and TDP grows 3.3 times. Second panel shows the dense FP16 off-chip balance point rising from 29 floating-point operations per byte transferred from HBM on P100 to 295 on H100 and 281 on B200."}

### Why Accelerators Coupled the Hardware and Software Stacks

This divergence between arithmetic density and memory supply erodes the classical separation of concerns inside an accelerator design. The reuse that keeps the arrays fed depends on the dataflow, the on-chip memory, and the compiler schedule at once. A conventional processor stack lets compiler writers, microarchitects, and process engineers work against relatively independent interfaces. @fig-tao-vs-taos contrasts that modular hierarchy with the coupled regime of domain-specific hardware, in which a single power, thermal, and area envelope ties all three layers together.

![**Specialization makes cross-layer dependencies explicit.** (a) A classical layered view separates optimization, architecture, and technology into modular tiers. (b) The specialization-coupled view reveals how domain specialization binds software mapping, microarchitecture, and silicon fabrication across shared power, thermal, and area constraints.](images/fig-tao-vs-taos){#fig-tao-vs-taos width="80%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side stack diagrams. The first panel shows optimization, architecture, and technology stacked in a top-down hierarchy. The second panel introduces a specialization block coupled across all three tiers, bounded by a shared thermal, power, and area constraint perimeter."}

Specialization does not invent cross-layer coupling, but it removes the slack that once hid it. An architect who chooses a systolic or tensor-core array geometry fixes which dataflows keep operands local. Sizing the on-chip scratchpad to sustain that reuse then sets die area and wire reach, and those layout choices determine clock frequency and leakage in the chosen process node. An architectural model that evaluates datapath throughput without accounting for on-chip storage area and physical wire delay can misrank candidates inside the block. Even when a block's internal datapath, storage, and wires are well balanced, however, its value still depends on how it fits into the surrounding system.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

## Balancing Specialization and System Composition

A specialized engine delivers a system speedup only when the surrounding machine can supply its inputs and use its outputs. The host still executes control flow, the runtime moves data and synchronizes execution, and shared memories and links serve other clients. The architect must therefore compare complete organizations, including the software and communication needed to use each block, before deciding which specialized capability is worth its area and power.

### From Kernel Efficiency to System Speedup

Specialization can produce large local gains by removing general-purpose machinery. For the H.264 video encoder studied by @HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency, a fixed-function application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) improved kernel energy efficiency roughly 500-fold relative to a four-core chip multiprocessor. @fig-ch02-specialization-energy traces that gain through each step toward the ASIC and shows where the base processors spent their energy.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Base-processor energy shares from Hameed et al. Table 3, summed across the four encoder stages.
import csv as _csv2he
from pathlib import Path as _Path2he
import _python.plots as _ap2he

_he_path = _Path2he(_ap2he.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-hameed-component-breakdown.csv"
with open(_he_path, encoding="utf-8") as _fh:
    _he_rows = [r for r in _csv2he.DictReader(l for l in _fh if not l.startswith("#"))
                if r["optimization_stage"] == "base_RISC_CMP" and r["metric"] == "energy_mJ_per_frame"
                and r["evidence_class"] == "transcribed" and r["component"] != "Total" and r["h264_substage"] != "Total"]
_he_tot = {}
for _r in _he_rows:
    _he_tot[_r["component"]] = _he_tot.get(_r["component"], 0.0) + float(_r["value"])
_he_all = sum(_he_tot.values())
he_fu_pct = f"{100 * _he_tot['FU'] / _he_all:.1f}"
he_if_pct = f"{100 * _he_tot['IF'] / _he_all:.1f}"
he_table_ratio = f"{_he_all / 4:.0f}"
```

![**Most of the efficiency gap lies outside the arithmetic.** (a) Energy efficiency of a 720p H.264 encoder as a four-processor 90\ nm chip gains single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) and very-long-instruction-word (VLIW) instructions, fused operations, and custom instructions, compared with an ASIC, using the factors stated in the source's text; its tables give about `{python} he_table_ratio`$\times$ for the ASIC. (b) Base-processor energy by component across the encoder, as tabulated in the source [@HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency].](images/fig-ch02-specialization-energy){#fig-ch02-specialization-energy width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel horizontal bar chart. Panel (a) shows energy efficiency on a log scale relative to base processors: 7 times with SIMD and VLIW, 10 times with operation fusion, 170 times with custom instructions, and 500 times for the ASIC. Panel (b) shows base-processor energy shares: instruction fetch 33.6 percent, pipeline registers 22.0 percent, data cache 19.2 percent, control 9.7 percent, register file 9.7 percent, and functional units 5.8 percent."}

Functional units account for only `{python} he_fu_pct`% of the base processors' energy, while instruction fetch alone takes `{python} he_if_pct`%. Wider datapaths and fused operations therefore recover only about one order of magnitude. The larger gains arrive once custom instructions and fixed logic remove the cost of fetching, decoding, and sequencing each operation. That result explains the attraction of specialization, but the fraction of the application accelerated and the cost of reaching the block determine how much benefit survives in a full system.

Amdahl's law makes this distinction explicit. If a fraction $f$ of baseline execution receives a local speedup $S_{\mathrm{accel}}$, the total speedup including communication is

$$S_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \frac{f}{S_{\mathrm{accel}}} + t_{\mathrm{comm}}}$${#eq-amdahl-communication}

where $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is the added, nonoverlapped transfer and synchronization time normalized to baseline execution time. Even with free communication, an infinitely fast accelerator cannot exceed $1/(1-f)$ total speedup because the unaccelerated host work in @eq-amdahl-communication remains [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]; communication lowers that ceiling further.

How strongly this bound limits a design depends on the workload. Under Gustafson's law, a system can increase its parallel work as more processors become available, as a training study might do with a larger model or dataset [@Gustafson1988AmdahlLaw]. A latency-critical mobile extended-reality (XR) pipeline instead has fixed per-frame work and a deadline. Dispatch and synchronization consume time that extra arithmetic units cannot recover.

The LogCA accelerator model separates the costs hidden inside the communication term [@AltafWood2017LogCA]. The useful distinction here is between a fixed cost paid for each invocation and a data-transfer cost that grows with the work. For a simple offload with no overlap, completion time is the sum of invocation time, accelerator execution time, and transfer time. Offloading helps only when that sum is smaller than execution on an optimized host.

Consider a neural processing unit (NPU) invoked separately for each small layer of a neural network. Command preparation, queue submission, and synchronization can consume much of the elapsed time even when the matrix arithmetic finishes quickly. Fusing layers or batching requests places more useful work behind each launch and can move the workload beyond its break-even payload size. But batching alone cannot remove a transfer cost that grows in proportion to the arithmetic. If moving each additional operation's data takes at least as much time as offloading saves on that operation, no larger payload makes the nonoverlapped offload profitable. The design needs fewer transferred bytes, more link bandwidth, or effective overlap.

These remedies cross different boundaries. A compiler may retain intermediate tensors on chip and reduce traffic without changing the interface. A lower-cost submission path changes how the runtime invokes the accelerator, while a wider physical link changes the hardware. The actual launch path, achieved bandwidth, data reuse, and host baseline determine which remedy helps; a link specification alone cannot settle the comparison. An empirical sweep across payload sizes tests where, if anywhere, the complete offload becomes faster than host execution.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Crossovers from the retained three-run sweep: data/studies/27-offload-break-even/summary.json
import json as _json2ob
from pathlib import Path as _Path2ob
import _python.plots as _ap2ob

_ob = _json2ob.loads(
    (_Path2ob(_ap2ob.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "27-offload-break-even" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
_ob_x = _ob["crossovers"]


def _ob_range(arm):
    runs = _ob_x[arm]["per_run_n"]
    return f"{min(runs):,}" if min(runs) == max(runs) else f"{min(runs):,} and {max(runs):,}"


ob_res = _ob_range("mps_resident")
ob_copy = _ob_range("mps_copy")
ob_sixteen = _ob_range("mps_16_launch")
ob_one = _ob_range("mps_bmm")
ob_runs = len(_ob_x["mps_bmm"]["per_run_n"])
assert _ob_x["mps_16_launch"]["stable_across_runs"] and _ob_x["mps_bmm"]["stable_across_runs"]
```

Our sweep on one Apple-silicon laptop times 32-bit floating-point matrix products on the CPU, through its vendor library, and on the integrated GPU, through PyTorch (@fig-ch02-offload-break-even). Across `{python} ob_runs` independent runs, a single $n \times n$ product first beat the host at $n$ between `{python} ob_res`, whether its operands already sat on the GPU or were copied in and out. Batching lowered the break-even. Sixteen products beat the host at $n$ of `{python} ob_sixteen` as separate launches and `{python} ob_one` as one launch.

![**Launch cost sets a floor, and batching moves the break-even toward smaller matrices.** Median time for 32-bit floating-point matrix products on an Apple M5 Max in three independent runs, each drawn as its own line: (a) one product on the host CPU and on the GPU, with operands resident or copied in and out; (b) sixteen products on the host and on the GPU as separate launches or one launch. CPU and GPU share memory here, so the copies do not cross a discrete link. Crossovers describe this one machine.](images/fig-ch02-offload-break-even){#fig-ch02-offload-break-even width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel log-log line chart of median time against matrix dimension from 16 to 3072, with three lines per series for three runs. In both panels the host CPU rises steadily from about a microsecond or tens of microseconds, while GPU series stay flat near 0.2 to 0.6 milliseconds and then rise, crossing below the host between dimensions of about 256 and 1024."}

The GPU's flat floor at small sizes is the fixed invocation cost that LogCA isolates, and only enough work behind one launch can repay it. The sweep supports the direction of each remedy without supplying a design constant. The batched crossovers repeated exactly, whereas the single-product crossovers moved by a full step of the size grid between runs, a shift that one run cannot reveal. Shared memory also leaves untested the transfer cost that grows with the work, the case in which no payload size reaches break-even.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The unamortized offload wall"}
**The trap.** A team treats the local matrix-multiply acceleration of an NPU as the expected system speedup.

**The mechanism.** Small layers may contain too little work to amortize each invocation, while input and output transfers add costs that grow with the workload. An optimized host can also erase an apparent gain measured against scalar code.

**The lesson.** Compare complete offloads against optimized host execution. Test whether fusion, batching, local reuse, or a cheaper submission path changes the result. If feasible changes still leave the offload below break-even, retaining host execution is the supported choice.
:::

The offload comparison thus requires more than a faster datapath. It needs a workable mapping and invocation path, and it may require changing the boundary between software and hardware. Integrating the resulting blocks adds a further set of physical and behavioral constraints.

### Packaging and Wafer-Scale Communication {#sec-wafer-scale-communication-tradeoffs}

Partitioning a large design into chiplets can improve manufacturing yield under random-defect models, let different functions use separate process nodes, and spread development cost across products. Those benefits must pay for packaging, test, assembly losses, and die-to-die communication [@Murphy1964CostSize; @FengMa2022ChipletActuary]. A partition that looks favorable in a block diagram may require more bandwidth than the available die edge can carry. The bandwidth available per unit of edge, or *shoreline bandwidth density*, depends on interface placement, connection pitch, and signaling rate, so the partition and the package have to be evaluated together.

Standard interfaces reduce part of the integration burden. Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) specifies die-to-die physical layers and protocols [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec], and a test standard lets defective chiplets be screened before assembly [@IEEE2020Std1838]. Neither establishes that the finished system has enough power, cooling, or bandwidth, and screened chiplets can still carry undetected defects or fail in assembly.

Keeping compute and storage on a wafer changes these trade-offs rather than removing them. The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine keeps communication on a large compute and SRAM fabric [@Cerebras2019WSE], reducing reliance on board-level links while requiring specialized power delivery, cooling, and defect tolerance. In a wafer-scale GPU case study, physical constraints reduced usable capacity from a nominal 100 GPU modules to 40 [@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU]. Available silicon area therefore does not directly determine usable compute; placement, defect routing, and software scheduling determine which resources a workload can exploit.

Composition also creates failures that do not appear when blocks are checked separately. Third-party intellectual property (IP) delivered as hard macros, already laid out and fixed, or as encrypted RTL restricts integration teams to documented behavior, supplied models, and accessible interfaces [@Arm2013CortexA15HardMacro; @Intel2024EncryptedRTLIP]. Even when blocks implement a standard bus [@Arm2020AXI], incompatible assumptions about reset order, power-up sequence, or clock domains can prevent them from operating together. A search cannot safely treat missing compatibility information as permission to combine blocks, and obtaining that information consumes engineering time before performance evaluation can begin.

### Choosing the System Boundary

The same composition problem extends beyond a package. A candidate accelerator may finish its own kernel sooner yet send enough extra traffic across a shared fabric to delay the end-to-end request. Whenever an interaction can reverse which design wins, the evaluation boundary must include it. The progression from cores to warehouse-scale systems in @fig-architecture-levers identifies the additional obligations that arise as that boundary expands.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The tall print-size scale diagram needs a full-page float option near its discussion. -->
![**The study boundary must include interactions that can change the decision.** Stacked from warehouse-scale deployment at the top down to core execution at the bottom, five compute scales illustrate how comparison obligations funnel outward as the system boundary expands upward from a core. A broader study may reuse component models; it need not reproduce every lower-level detail at the same fidelity.](images/fig-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram of five architecture scales stacked from warehouse-scale system at the top down through wafer-scale system, system-on-chip or chiplet, accelerator, and core at the bottom, funneling outward as the system boundary expands upward from core to warehouse-scale. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path feeding one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

At warehouse scale, placement and sharing decisions couple servers, networks, distributed runtimes, cooling, and facility power [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Within and across nodes, cache-coherent interconnects such as Compute Express Link (CXL) make pooled memory another architectural choice [@CXLConsortium2026CXL]. These mechanisms belong inside the study when they can change its target metric, whether tail latency, sustained throughput, or total cost.

A broader boundary does not require cycle-level simulation of every component. Architects combine characterized component models with trace-driven or discrete-event simulation, hardware testbeds, and production telemetry. The combination must preserve the relevant interactions. Independent trace replays can miss shared-network contention, while mean response times hide stragglers that govern tail latency at scale [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale]. Choosing the smallest boundary that captures effects capable of reversing the decision limits evaluation cost without assuming those effects away.

Within that boundary, a hardware organization still needs software that can use it. The offload example shows why compiler mappings and runtime behavior belong in the comparison, and why changing either can alter the value of hardware that is already fixed.

## Workload Volatility and Software–Hardware Coupling

A compiler can fuse operations into a payload large enough to amortize an accelerator launch, or introduce spills that erase the expected saving. The evaluation therefore needs an executable path to compile, schedule, and drive the candidate hardware. That path continues to change after silicon is fixed, creating two related pressures: making a specialized mechanism usable and keeping it useful as workloads evolve.

### Why Hardware Gains Require a Working Compiler Path

A custom matrix unit or instruction extension can excel in a hand-coded microbenchmark yet remain idle in an application if no compiler pass, kernel library, or runtime can use it effectively. An *executable software path* connects the programming model through compilation and libraries to the runtime, driver or firmware, and deployment controls. Different systems require different components, but the path must be complete enough to run the intended workload without losing the hardware benefit to extra transfers, spills, or dispatch overhead.

Building that path separately for every target would repeat most of the work. A *compiler narrow waist* shares part of it through an intermediate representation (IR). Common transformations operate on the IR, while target-specific lowering maps operations onto a particular machine. Halide separates an algorithm from its execution schedule [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM]; Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) supports transformations across levels of abstraction [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR].[^fn-mlir-dialects-c02] These abstractions reduce duplication, but every target still needs lowering, runtime support, and validation suited to its hardware.

[^fn-mlir-dialects-c02]: **MLIR dialects**: MLIR groups operations into modular dialects, each at one level of abstraction, from tensor algebra (`linalg`) through loops and arithmetic down to LLVM IR or hardware-specific dialects. A computation is lowered step by step through these dialects, so each optimization can run where the information it needs, such as tensor shapes or loop bounds, is still explicit.

The path in @fig-codegen-narrow-waist locates that shared representation between source programs and target execution. A matrix instruction needs a lowering path that matches its operand layout; an asynchronous transfer engine needs scheduling and synchronization that preserve correctness. Those obligations connect compiler work directly to whether an architectural candidate can be evaluated at all.

![**Executable target software paths connect developer intent to verification checks.** High-level domain-specific abstract syntax trees (Python, Triton domain-specific languages) lower through mid-level control-data flow graphs in MLIR dialects and LLVM IR at the compiler narrow waist, where workload intent, architectural mechanisms such as CPU instruction-set extensions and NPU dataflows, and silicon constraints converge. Lowered machine code and runtimes then pass through verification checks for correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability.](images/fig-codegen-narrow-waist){#fig-codegen-narrow-waist width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of an executable target software path showing programming models, compiler representations, libraries, runtimes, and generated code connecting hardware constraints to correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability checks."}

The software that exposes hardware capabilities also keeps growing (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall). CUTLASS's architecture-specific headers accumulate templates and inline assembly for specialized instructions [@NVIDIACUTLASS], Triton's source trees span a shared compiler, target-specific lowering, runtime interfaces, and vendored headers [@TilletEtAl2019Triton], and serving frameworks such as vLLM maintain their own native kernel libraries [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention].

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The readable stacked panels and caption were deferred several pages under top-only placement. -->
![**Software source trees document an expanding implementation footprint.** Newline counts measured at release tags show (a) CUTLASS architecture-specific headers reaching about 208,000 lines and inline `asm volatile` statements passing 3,000; (b) Triton's selected trees reaching about 280,000 lines, including vendored headers, examples, and tests; and (c) vLLM native kernels reaching about 120,000 lines [@NVIDIACUTLASS; @TilletEtAl2019Triton; @KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. Directory reorganizations limit comparisons of subcategories; these counts do not measure maintenance cost.](images/fig-ch09-software-porting-wall){#fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Three-panel bar chart of source lines at selected release tags. CUTLASS headers grow to about 690 thousand lines, including about 208 thousand architecture-specific lines, and inline assembly statements exceed 3,000. Triton's selected source trees total about 86 thousand lines at v1, fall at v2, and rise to about 280 thousand at v3.7; totals include vendored headers, examples, and tests. vLLM native kernel sources grow to about 120 thousand lines, with a directory reorganization at v0.27."}

Each new hardware mechanism therefore carries a software development and maintenance cost. Shared compilers reduce duplication across targets, and hand-tuned libraries expose hardware features before general compilers support them, but both routes must still produce a working binary that the evaluation can run.

Once code reaches the target, its mapping can determine whether the offload pays. Fusing operations places more work behind each invocation, while retaining intermediate tensors on chip reduces traffic. These changes address the two distinct costs identified by LogCA. Yet fusion also keeps more values live at once, increasing register pressure. If those values exceed the available registers, the compiler spills them to memory and can undo the locality gain.

The RISC-V Vector extension makes the trade-off concrete. A compiler can group architectural vector registers to process more elements per instruction, but wider groups leave fewer independent groups for other live values [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. A fused kernel may therefore benefit from wide grouping until register spills add enough traffic to slow it down. Peak vector width cannot determine the winner; compiled execution with the intended data types and workload can.

An autotuner such as AutoTVM searches compiler schedules on a fixed machine [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. A joint hardware–software study varies the machine as well, so each hardware–schedule pair needs a fair evaluation. Holding one candidate's schedule fixed while tuning another can mistake software effort for architectural merit. Producing and checking the executable paths is thus part of the cost of comparing hardware alternatives, rather than a step that follows the architecture decision.

### Changing Software and Fixed Hardware {#sec-software-changes-faster-than-silicon}

An architectural comparison may become outdated while a chip is still being specified, verified, and fabricated. A memory hierarchy tuned for one model family and compiler release can encounter different tensor shapes, kernel schedules, and serving regimes at deployment. Before tapeout, hardware and software teams can revise the design together, although late hardware changes become expensive. After tapeout, software has to adapt the fixed machine.

Numerical formats make this commitment especially clear. Supporting FP8, 4-bit integer, or block-scale representations changes the arithmetic units and datapaths built into silicon. Block-scale formats share exponent or scale metadata across groups of elements [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling], so their efficiency depends on a specific organization of values and metadata. A model that adopts a different format after the datapath is frozen may no longer use the hardware as efficiently. The architect must decide which workload properties are stable enough to specialize and where programmability is worth its area and energy cost.

Memory behavior can change just as sharply. Convolutional inference with fixed frame sizes follows a relatively regular schedule, whereas autoregressive Transformer serving retains a growing key-value (KV) cache of attention keys and values from earlier tokens to avoid recomputing them [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. Variable sequence lengths change the amount of stored state. Mixture-of-experts models route inputs to selected expert subnetworks [@ShazeerEtAl2017MoE], making traffic depend on the input, while prompt processing and incremental token generation form distinct prefill and decode phases [@AgrawalEtAl2024SarathiServe]. These changes alter how computation and memory traffic arrive. A larger working set can overflow a scratchpad and force transfers to dynamic random-access memory (DRAM); a smaller serving batch can leave too little work to amortize each accelerator invocation. The relevant question is which assumption changed and whether the hardware retains enough flexibility to accommodate it.

Compute demand is moving just as quickly. Epoch AI reported a four- to fivefold annual increase in training compute for notable models through May 2024 [@SevillaRoldan2024ComputeGrowth]. A frozen July 2026 snapshot of the same database shows the trend (@fig-training-compute-growth) [@EpochAI2025AIModels].

```{python}
#| label: fig-training-compute-growth
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Reported and estimated training compute rises about 4.4-fold per year in this historical sample.**
#|   The 467 displayed records come from a frozen July 2026 snapshot of the Epoch AI database [@EpochAI2025AIModels].
#|   Compute is plotted logarithmically against publication date (2010–2026); it combines reported figures with
#|   source estimates of differing confidence, including speculative estimates. Filled points use the snapshot's
#|   frontier flag (top ten by training compute at release), and landmark systems are labeled. The line is an
#|   unweighted least-squares fit to the logarithm of compute. Its $\approx 4.4\times$ annual growth factor
#|   characterizes this sample and does not measure how changes in model scale intersect hardware development schedules.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale scatter plot of 467 reported or source-estimated AI training-compute values versus publication date from 2010 to 2026. Filled points mark the snapshot's frontier models. An unweighted fitted line marks roughly 4.4-fold growth per year. AlexNet, AlphaGo Zero, GPT-3, and GPT-4 are labeled; all records used in the fit are visible."

import csv
import datetime
import math
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _year(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-training-compute.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for row in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        yr = _year(row["publication_date"])
        try:
            flop = float(row["training_compute_flop"])
        except ValueError:
            flop = None
        if yr and flop and flop > 0 and 2010 <= yr <= 2026.6:
            pts.append({"yr": yr, "flop": flop, "name": row["model"], "frontier": row["frontier"] == "1"})

years = np.array([p["yr"] for p in pts])
logf = np.array([math.log10(p["flop"]) for p in pts])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(years, logf, 1)
growth = 10 ** slope

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.3))
other = [p for p in pts if not p["frontier"]]
front = [p for p in pts if p["frontier"]]
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in other], [p["flop"] for p in other], s=8, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=2, label="Notable models")
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in front], [p["flop"] for p in front], s=12, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["workload"], edgecolor=COLORS["workload_ink"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=3, label="Frontier models")
xline = np.array([2010, 2026.5])
ax.plot(xline, 10 ** (intercept + slope * xline), color=COLORS["constraints"], lw=1.5, zorder=4)
ax.text(2018.0, 10 ** (intercept + slope * 2018.8), f"×{growth:.1f} per year", fontsize=6.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], rotation=29, rotation_mode="anchor",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9))

by_name = {p["name"]: p for p in pts}
landmarks = {"AlexNet": ("AlexNet", 6, -12), "AlphaGo Zero": ("AlphaGo Zero", -8, 11),
             "GPT-3 175B (davinci)": ("GPT-3", -8, 11), "GPT-4 (Jun 2023)": ("GPT-4", 6, 10)}
for key, (label, dx, dy) in landmarks.items():
    p = by_name.get(key)
    if p:
        ax.annotate(label, (p["yr"], p["flop"]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy),
                    fontsize=5.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["muted"], lw=0.45))

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(2010, 2026.7)
ax.set_ylim(5e13, 3e27)
ax.set_xlabel("Publication date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Reported or estimated training compute (FLOP)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2010, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022, 2025])
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_spine].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.14, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

Larger training runs do not automatically change the underlying kernel mix, but performance measured at one model scale or serving regime does not transfer to another without re-evaluating memory traffic and software assumptions.

Deployment requirements can also change delivered throughput without changing the arithmetic or hardware. The matched MLPerf submissions below isolate one such pressure by comparing standard and interactive latency requirements on the same systems.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json as _json2ml
from pathlib import Path as _Path2ml
import _python.plots as _ap2ml

_ml12 = _json2ml.loads(
    (_Path2ml(_ap2ml.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
     / "data" / "studies" / "12-mlperf-latency-contract" / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
ml12_pairs = _ml12["pairs"]
ml12_logs = _ml12["raw_logs"]
ml12_std_ttft = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['standard_ttft_ms']):,}"
ml12_std_tpot = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['standard_tpot_ms']):,}"
ml12_int_ttft = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_ttft_ms']):,}"
ml12_int_tpot = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_tpot_ms']):,}"
ml12_min_pct = f"{100 * _ml12['minimum_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
```
