The matched set contains `{python} ml12_pairs` single-node, eight-accelerator Llama 2 70B server submissions in MLPerf Inference v5.0 [@MLCommons2025InferenceV50Results]. The Interactive scenario tightens 99th-percentile latency bounds from `{python} ml12_std_ttft`\ ms time to first token and `{python} ml12_std_tpot`\ ms time per output token (Standard) to `{python} ml12_int_ttft`\ ms and `{python} ml12_int_tpot`\ ms. Under those bounds, interactive server throughput falls to `{python} ml12_min_pct`% to `{python} ml12_max_pct`% of standard throughput (median `{python} ml12_med_pct`%), by a different fraction on each system (@fig-ch09-mlperf-latency-contract). The hardware has not changed, but the acceptable service behavior has. A throughput result established under the looser requirement cannot answer the stricter design question.

![**Submitted server throughput drops under a stricter latency contract on matched eight-accelerator systems.** Paired MLPerf Inference v5.0 closed submissions (`{python} ml12_pairs` system pairs, `{python} ml12_logs` logs) for eight-accelerator Llama 2 70B servers [@MLCommons2025InferenceV50Results]: (a) 99th-percentile latency targets under Standard (`{python} ml12_std_ttft`\ ms first token / `{python} ml12_std_tpot`\ ms per output token) versus Interactive (`{python} ml12_int_ttft`\ ms / `{python} ml12_int_tpot`\ ms) contracts, and (b) submitted Interactive throughput as a share of Standard across H100, H200, and B200 pairs (`{python} ml12_min_pct`% to `{python} ml12_max_pct`%, median `{python} ml12_med_pct`%).](images/fig-ch09-mlperf-latency-contract){#fig-ch09-mlperf-latency-contract width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel horizontal bar chart of 19 matched eight-accelerator Llama 2 70B server pairs in MLPerf Inference v5.0. Panel (a) compares the 99th-percentile latency targets in milliseconds between the Standard contract (2,000 milliseconds first token and 200 milliseconds per output token) and the Interactive contract (450 milliseconds and 40 milliseconds). Panel (b) plots Interactive throughput as a percentage of Standard throughput across 19 NVIDIA H100 SXM, H200 NVL, H200 SXM, and B200 SXM system pairs, ranging from 42.0 percent to 63.9 percent with a median of 58.8 percent."}

A changed requirement defines a different task, not a better implementation of the old one. A faster kernel for the original workload can strengthen the case for existing hardware; a new model shape, accuracy target, or latency requirement changes what the machine must accomplish. Standardized benchmarks hold tasks and run rules fixed long enough to compare systems. Within a single MLPerf version, division, scenario, and accuracy target, teams can optimize their software while retaining a defined comparison [@ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. Once those conditions change, earlier measurements may need to be repeated.

Even a label such as mobile XR leaves much unspecified. Sensor fusion, head tracking, and neural rendering impose different deadlines and memory-access patterns across a system-on-chip (SoC). An XRBench workload [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] still needs exact traces, model versions, and quality targets before it can distinguish candidate hardware. Fixing those inputs makes a comparison meaningful, but the hardware parameters and software mappings within it can still produce far more alternatives than the team can evaluate in detail.

## Why Coupled Design Spaces Outgrow Manual Search {#sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search}

Hardware parameters, dataflow mappings, and compiler schedules multiply the number of candidate designs within a study. That count alone says little about the work required to compare them. An analytical model may score a large space cheaply, while a much smaller set of candidates can consume the available budget if each requires detailed simulation, physical implementation, and new verification work.

Timeloop, an analytical framework for mapping and evaluating deep neural network (DNN) accelerators, illustrates the combinatorial growth [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. A convolutional layer has loops over batches, channels, output positions, and kernel positions. Each memory level introduces choices about how to order and divide those loops and which tensors to retain. A change in buffer capacity can make one mapping legal and another impossible, so the best mapping depends on the hardware being evaluated. The architect is searching coupled hardware and software choices even for one layer.

Practical exploration therefore eliminates illegal configurations, screens survivors with inexpensive models, and develops selected candidates far enough to run stronger checks. The published tasks in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors illustrate different costs along that path. Mapping and compiler tuning create many alternatives within a fixed machine; accelerator design-space exploration (DSE) and floorplanning also change the implementation that later checks must assess.

| **Architecture task** | **Scale anchor** | **Why candidate count is not enough** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DNN accelerator mapping | Timeloop enumerates loop permutations, factorization choices, and level-bypass alternatives [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. | Mapping is itself a combinatorial problem; architecture evaluation depends on the mapper and its constraints. |
| DNN accelerator DSE | MAESTRO, an analytical cost model for estimating DNN dataflow performance, reports 480M candidates, 2.5M valid designs, and 0.17M designs/s [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. | Pruning rules determine which candidates are evaluated and which are never seen. |
| Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) block floorplanning | AlphaChip uses reinforcement learning to generate macro placements [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. | Reported gains depend on the cases, baselines, compute budgets, and downstream checks; a reproduction, the authors' reply, and an updated assessment still dispute whether the baselines were matched [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. |
| Tensor-program tuning | AutoTVM, a machine learning-based tensor program optimizer, describes tensor-operator search spaces on the order of billions of possible implementations for a single GPU operator [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. | Compiler schedules create a hardware-dependent search problem of their own. |
: **Large search spaces place different demands on evaluation.** The four tasks differ in candidate scale, validity constraints, feedback cost, and evidence requirements. {#tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

\FloatBarrier

The MAESTRO result illustrates why a large count does not establish a need for a learned search method. Its analytical model evaluates dataflow choices quickly, although its rankings still depend on the workload and the physical effects represented by the model. Macro placement faces a different limit. Proposing coordinates does not establish that the resulting floorplan can be routed or meet timing. Both studies need selection, but they spend their evaluation budgets on different uncertainties.

The useful question is therefore how much work a candidate requires before it can inform a decision. Fast screening may make a broad search affordable, yet it cannot supply every fact about the finalists. Physical layout, realistic workload execution, and functional verification expose different reasons why a promising candidate may fail.

## Why Physical Layout, Simulation, and Verification Slow the Loop {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

A team can accelerate performance screening only to watch its preferred candidates fail timing closure or require more verification than the project can support. Physical implementation, workload simulation, and functional verification resolve different uncertainties, and each needs inputs that an early architectural description may not yet contain. Their cost includes preparing those inputs and interpreting failures as well as running the tools.

### Physical Constraints {#sec-physical-constraints-move-into-architecture}

A high-level model may predict throughput from array dimensions and memory capacity without knowing where the arrays and memories will be placed. Placement and routing determine the wire lengths, capacitances, and congestion that affect realized timing and energy [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. A larger cache can reduce misses while requiring longer wires and more leakage power, as in the opening example. Moving to a newer process node does not settle the trade-off, because logic cells, SRAM macros (prebuilt memory blocks characterized for area, access time, and power), and interconnects scale differently. The comparison needs the area, access time, and energy of the memory actually available in that process.

The cost of moving data explains why these physical details can reverse a ranking based on arithmetic alone. In the 45\ nm reference values compiled by @Horowitz2014Energy, SRAM and DRAM accesses consume much more energy than a local integer addition (@fig-data-movement-energy-scale). The access widths and memory capacities differ, so these values illustrate the importance of locality rather than supplying an energy model for a current chip.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-movement-energy-scale
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Data movement can dominate arithmetic energy.** Reference $45\ \text{nm}$ energy values from @Horowitz2014Energy
#|   demonstrate a disparity of more than four orders of magnitude between local arithmetic (0.1\ pJ for a 32-bit integer add)
#|   and memory access (10–100\ pJ for on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM), 1.3–2.6\ nJ for off-chip DRAM, a $13{,}000\text{--}26{,}000\times$
#|   energy penalty). Architectural comparisons must represent data locality, buffer hierarchies, and memory
#|   traffic rather than counting arithmetic operations in isolation. Transcribed order-of-magnitude anchors,
#|   not current-node device estimates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale plot comparing arithmetic and memory-access energy, showing a 32-bit integer add at 0.1 picojoules, static random-access memory (SRAM) accesses from 10 to 100 picojoules, and an off-chip DRAM access range from 1.3 to 2.6 nanojoules."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style, draw_range_rows, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Source dataset: data/datasets/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, 45 nm).
# Values are read from the CSV; ratios to the 32-bit integer add are computed here.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    src = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))]

baseline = float(src[0]["energy_low_pj"])


def _fmt_ratio(value):
    ratio = value / baseline
    return f"{ratio / 1000:.0f}k" if ratio >= 1000 and value >= 1000 else f"{ratio:.0f}"


rows = []
for r in src:
    low, high = float(r["energy_low_pj"]), float(r["energy_high_pj"])
    op, width = r["operation_or_access"], r["width_or_capacity"]
    if "SRAM" in op:
        capacity = width.replace(" 64 bit", "")
        label, note = f"{capacity} SRAM access", "64b access"
        color = COLORS["orange"] if high >= 100 else COLORS["green"]
    elif "DRAM" in op:
        label, note, color = "off-chip DRAM access", "64b access", COLORS["red"]
    else:
        label, note, color = f"{width.replace(' bit', 'b')} {op}", "local arithmetic", COLORS["blue"]
    right = f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}$\\times$" if low == high else f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}–{_fmt_ratio(high)}$\\times$"
    rows.append({"display_label": label, "display_note": note, "energy_low_pj": low,
                 "energy_high_pj": high, "right_label": right, "color": color})

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 3.2))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.40, right=0.80, top=0.82, bottom=0.08)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(0.06, 4000),
    xticks=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
    xticklabels=["0.1 pJ", "1 pJ", "10 pJ", "100 pJ", "1 nJ"],
    xlabel="rough energy per operation or access",
)
draw_range_rows(ax, rows, low_key="energy_low_pj", high_key="energy_high_pj", label_x=-0.82, right_x=1.04, label_fontsize=6.6, note_fontsize=5.4, right_fontsize=6.1, label_dy=-0.17, note_dy=0.23)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The large separation between local arithmetic and memory access means that reducing an operation count can still increase energy if the new mapping sends more operands off chip. A system estimate must combine the workload's actual traffic with costs characterized for its implementation. The following decomposition keeps those contributions explicit:

$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} = E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} + E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
$${#eq-system-energy-decomposition}

In @eq-system-energy-decomposition, a decrease in compute energy is beneficial only if it exceeds any increases in the other terms. The memory term depends on how often the workload reaches each level of the hierarchy, much as the memory wall depends on access frequency and the latency the processor can hide [@WulfMcKee1995HittingMemoryWall].

Data movement between tiles also imposes latency and layout constraints beyond its energy cost. At runtime, overloaded links cause queueing and backpressure; during layout, the chosen network must fit within the available metal routing tracks. Runtime network congestion and physical routing congestion are distinct effects, although the floorplan can influence both.

Power delivery and heat removal add constraints that average energy cannot capture. When many execution units switch on together, a rapid current increase across the resistance and inductance of the supply network can lower the voltage reaching the cells. That transient droop may slow them enough to cause a timing failure. Sustained activity instead raises the question of whether the package can remove heat from where it is generated. In stacked designs, the position of active logic and the heat-removal path matter alongside total power. A thermal estimate therefore cannot establish that a rapid electrical transient is harmless.

Stronger checks need more information because they resolve those specific mechanisms. A timing analysis needs characterized cell delays, clock constraints, and wire estimates; a thermal analysis needs the placement of heat sources and package conditions. Timing must also be checked across specified operating modes, such as low-power and full-speed settings, and across process, voltage, and temperature conditions [@Cadence2021Tempus], because manufacturing variation makes some transistors slower than others, and delay also shifts with supply voltage and temperature. A design that meets its cycle time under nominal conditions may fail under another required condition. Obtaining compatible libraries, memory macros, and package models is part of the evaluation cost even before the tools run.

Consider a floorplan search that ranks memory placements using a fast wirelength estimate. A compact placement may appear favorable yet crowd pins into a narrow routing channel. Detailed routing can then expose insufficient tracks, spacing violations, or delays that the proxy omitted. The failure does not automatically identify a bad architecture, because the constraints or tool setup may also be wrong. Engineers must determine which explanation applies before deciding whether to repair the setup, revise the candidate, or broaden the search.

More detailed analysis earns its cost when it answers a question that could change the decision. Physical checks do not replace the separate need to run representative workloads and establish correct behavior. A microarchitecture can lead on advertised core counts and clock rates yet fall behind on real workloads once threads contend for shared structures and power limits cap frequency, as one AMD processor generation showed [@ButlerEtAl2011Bulldozer].

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** In the Bulldozer generation (Zambezi, 2011), AMD grouped two integer cores behind a shared front end and floating-point unit while pushing clock frequency hard [@ButlerEtAl2011Bulldozer]. Core counts and frequencies are easy to advertise, so they made compelling marketing points. In sharing those structures, the design team traded per-thread capacity for aggregate throughput.

**The gap.** Those figures did not reflect how real workloads used the machine. The shared structures became bottlenecks when threads competed for them, and the higher frequencies raised power draw. The later FX-9590 part carried a 220\ W TDP [@AMDFXQuickReference].

**The lesson.** Core count and clock rate alone cannot settle the comparison. Shared structures must be evaluated with workloads that expose contention, alongside power and frequency behavior. AMD's later Zen design placed renewed emphasis on per-core performance and efficiency [@AMDZen].
:::

### Simulation Throughput and Fidelity

Detailed performance simulation exposes resource conflicts that simple models omit, but it executes much more slowly than native hardware. The 2013 zsim study reported detailed gem5, Flexus, and MARSS configurations running at about two hundred thousand target instructions per host second [@ZSim]. That historical rate is not a prediction for a current study; it shows why architects must measure their own simulator throughput before committing to workload lengths and candidate counts.

Faster execution often requires more setup or a different representation, a trade-off that @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces develops. FireSim, for example, uses field-programmable gate array (FPGA) acceleration for full-system, cycle-exact RTL simulation [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Preparing an FPGA model costs effort, and cycle-exact RTL execution still omits routed wire delays and package thermals. The choice depends on which behavior must be represented and how many runs can reuse the setup.

Sampling reduces runtime by selecting representative parts of a program. SimPoint selects program regions [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], while SMARTS uses statistical sampling with explicit error bounds [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The saving depends on how well those regions represent the workload and whether caches and branch predictors hold realistic state when each measured region begins. Analytical screening, sampled detailed simulation, and full-workload execution can therefore serve different stages of a comparison, with each retaining uncertainty that later work may need to resolve.

A coarse filter can discard a promising candidate or send an unsuitable one into an expensive run. Even a careful full-workload performance study, however, exercises only the behaviors reached by its inputs. It does not establish correctness across the legal state transitions that the design permits.

### Verification Bottlenecks

Verification is demanding because sequential storage creates a large space of possible states. A design with $n$ state bits can encode up to $2^n$ configurations. Reset and legal transitions restrict the reachable subset, but realistic processors and accelerators still have too many behaviors to check by brute-force enumeration. Changing a pipeline, cache protocol, or interface can introduce new interactions even when most of the implementation is reused.

Tests exercise selected behaviors under supplied inputs, whereas a completed formal proof establishes a stated property for all behaviors covered by its model and assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]; bounded checks and functional coverage make narrower claims, which @sec-feedback-verification-trust develops. Stronger claims therefore require broader checks, suitable assumptions, and enough time for the tools and engineers to complete them.

Verification effort belongs beside power, performance, and area (PPA) in an architectural comparison. A cache-coherence shortcut may improve simulated throughput yet introduce transient states and races whose verification exceeds the program's budget.

Industry staffing surveys show where effort has concentrated. The 2022 Wilson Research Group study of integrated circuit (IC) and ASIC projects reports verification staffing growing at about 6.2% per year from 2007 to 2022, compared with about 2.7% for design staffing [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. The indexed series in @fig-verification-demand-scissors tracks project staffing, not the marginal cost of checking one more candidate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Verification staffing grew faster than design staffing.** Mean peak staffing per IC/ASIC project
#|   indexed to a 2007 baseline demonstrates that verification engineer demand grew by 146% (a 6.2%
#|   compound annual growth rate [CAGR], reaching $\approx 2.46\times$) from 2007 to 2022, while design engineer demand grew by 50%
#|   (a 2.7% CAGR, reaching $\approx 1.50\times$) [@Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Filled markers indicate
#|   printed data labels from published survey figures; hollow 2022 markers represent chart-read approximations
#|   constrained by the study's stated growth rates.
#| out-width: "100%"

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Mean peak engineers per IC/ASIC project, Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA
# functional-verification studies (Foster's published summaries).
# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv. Rows with
# evidence_type == chart_read_constrained are drawn hollow; growth labels are computed.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    staff = [r for r in csv.DictReader(fh) if r["year"].isdigit()]
years = [int(r["year"]) for r in staff]

verif = [float(r["verification_engineers_mean_peak"]) for r in staff]
printed = [r["evidence_type"] == "printed_data_label" for r in staff]

design_idx = [v / design[0] for v in design]
verif_idx = [v / verif[0] for v in verif]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.80, top=0.93, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(years, verif_idx, color=COLORS["green"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.plot(years, design_idx, color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
for x, v, d, solid in zip(years, verif_idx, design_idx, printed):
    if solid:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=22, color=COLORS["green"], zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=20, marker="s", color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=26, facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["green"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=24, marker="s", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["blue"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)

ax.text(years[-1] + 0.6, verif_idx[-1], f"verification\nengineers (+{(verif_idx[-1] - 1) * 100:.0f}%)",
        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["green"], clip_on=False)

        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["blue"], clip_on=False)

ax.set_xlim(years[0] - 1, years[-1] + 1)
ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.7)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_yticks([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1.0$\\times$", "1.5$\\times$", "2.0$\\times$", "2.5$\\times$"])
ax.set_ylabel(f"mean peak demand vs. {years[0]}", fontsize=7)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

```

Faster growth in verification staffing does not identify a single cause, but it shows why generating more candidates cannot be assumed to reduce engineering effort. A candidate that reuses a familiar interface may retain much of its test and proof infrastructure; a changed interface can require new properties, stimulus, and failure analysis. The cost depends on what changed and what assurance the decision requires.

Some of that work concerns behavior absent from ordinary performance models. A signal crossing asynchronous clock domains can violate a receiving register's timing requirements and enter a metastable state, an analog condition that a cycle-level testbench does not represent. Suitable synchronizers or transfer protocols reduce that risk, while checks must also establish that the surrounding logical communication remains correct. Clock-domain crossings are one of several mechanisms in industry respin reports, alongside logic flaws, timing, and hardware–firmware interactions [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. More random stimulus alone does not address every one of those mechanisms.

Escaped defects can require software workarounds that sacrifice performance or revised silicon. Intel's \$475M charge associated with the Pentium floating-point division defect illustrates the possible cost of a shipped arithmetic error [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge]. It does not establish a universal price for late defects, but it explains why teams spend substantial effort checking candidates before fabrication.

Generated hardware adds to this workload unless it arrives with usable, independently checked behavior. Published RTL-generation benchmarks report failures even at syntax parsing, interface compliance, and module-level functional testing [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. A passing module test still leaves system integration and physical checks. When the same model generates both the design and its tests, it can also reproduce the same misunderstanding in both. The Knight–Leveson experiment illustrated this correlated-failure problem [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. An independent reference or property that the generator cannot change is needed to expose such agreement on the wrong behavior.

The possible saving from a generated draft must therefore be compared with the work of integrating and checking it. Faster candidate creation helps when it removes missing implementation work; it can hinder progress when it consumes scarce verification capacity on additional failures. Physical implementation, software bring-up, and verification together determine how many alternatives a project can afford to develop.

\FloatBarrier

## The Economics of Specialized Silicon {#sec-design-cost-pressure}

Implementation, software, and verification consume a finite development budget. Much of this expense is non-recurring engineering (NRE), the upfront investment needed before volume production. Its scale influences both the architecture a program can justify and the number of alternatives it can develop far enough to compare.

Public estimates illustrate the investment without establishing a universal project price (@fig-design-cost-by-node). A 2018 International Business Strategies (IBS) series estimated IC design costs of \$51.3M at 28\ nm, \$297.8M at 7\ nm, and \$542.2M at 5\ nm [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm]. Arm's 2023 prospectus cites a July 2022 IBS series estimating \$249M at 7\ nm and \$725M at 2\ nm [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The two vintages disagree at 7\ nm, yet both place a substantial development investment behind leading-node specialization.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-by-node
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Leading-node design-cost estimates rise steeply, and they depend on the estimate's vintage.** Each bar is an
#|   International Business Strategies (IBS) estimate, labeled with the year of the IBS series it comes from
#|   [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm; @ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The two vintages differ at 7\ nm (\$298M versus \$249M),
#|   so the bars are published estimates under different assumptions, not a controlled node-scaling series or universal project prices.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of IC design-cost estimates by process node. The 2018 estimates are 51 million dollars at 28 nanometers, 298 million at 7 nanometers, and 542 million at 5 nanometers. The 2022 estimates, drawn hatched, are 249 million at 7 nanometers and 725 million at 2 nanometers."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv (rows with plotted == yes).
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")) if r["plotted"] == "yes"]
# Largest node first; within a node, older vintage first.
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (-float(r["node_nm"]), r["estimate_vintage"]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
positions = list(range(len(rows)))
for pos, r in zip(positions, rows):
    cost = float(r["cost_musd"])
    newer = r["estimate_vintage"].endswith("2022")
    ax.barh(pos, cost, height=0.58, color=COLORS["constraints_tint"], edgecolor=COLORS["constraints"],
            linewidth=1.4, hatch="////" if newer else None, zorder=3)
    ax.text(cost + 12, pos, f"${cost:,.0f}M", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7,
            fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], zorder=4)
    ax.text(cost + 100, pos, r["estimate_vintage"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6,
            color=COLORS["muted"], zorder=4)

ax.set_yticks(positions)
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{float(r['node_nm']):g} nm" for r in rows], fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 1000)
ax.set_xlabel("Estimated IC design cost (US$M)", fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
ax.grid(True, axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

That investment extends well beyond writing RTL. In the 2\ nm estimate cited by Arm, software development, verification, and IP qualification together account for 71% of the total [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The split describes one cost model, not the critical path of every program. It still shows that accelerating a local drafting task does not eliminate the surrounding work needed to ship the design. Assistance that creates more integration or verification work may move expense rather than reduce it.

Production volume determines how heavily development cost weighs on each shipped chip. In a simple accounting model,

$$
C_{\mathrm{unit}} = C_{\mathrm{variable}} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{NRE}}}{V},
$$

where $C_{\mathrm{variable}}$ is average manufacturing, packaging, and test cost per unit, $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ is allocated development investment, and $V$ is shipment volume. The model omits financing and time-to-market effects, but it explains why the same specialized design can be attractive at one volume and difficult to justify at another. Reusing qualified IP or a chiplet across products can spread the investment, while programmable engines retain flexibility at an area or energy cost.

For a mobile-XR program, the decision is whether custom silicon's efficiency and capability gains justify the hardware, software, and verification work at the anticipated volume. Retaining an existing processor, reusing more IP, or choosing a less expensive process may improve the economic balance while giving up performance or energy efficiency. These are architecture alternatives, not merely accounting adjustments after the design is chosen.

Evaluation itself consumes part of that finite budget. A detailed simulation or integration test can justify its expense when it resolves an uncertainty that would otherwise lead to costly redesign. More candidate generation is useful when it creates better options worth evaluating. Neither investment pays automatically; its value depends on the decision it improves and the total resources required to reach it.

## Locating the Bottleneck and Choosing Assistance {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

A design study encounters these pressures together. A different memory organization may need new compiler support, which changes traffic and the physical power comparison. One candidate may reuse existing tests, while another needs new properties and integration checks. The effort required to learn from an alternative depends on the work downstream of the proposal, so accelerating one step can expose a slower one elsewhere.

### Diagnosing the Work That Limits Progress

The limiting work is visible in a project's unfinished decisions. A team may be waiting for a workload trace, a characterized memory macro, an executable compiler path, or a verification engineer to diagnose a failure. Queue ages and lengths reveal where work accumulates; repeated runs reveal time lost to changed inputs or mistaken configurations. Industry trends help explain why these pressures arise, but only the program's own work can establish which one currently matters. In the Lighthouse cache study, the limiting work turns out to be a calibrated 3\ nm-class memory model rather than candidate generation (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces).

The MAESTRO example in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors shows why a fast optimizer may have little value when the work around it is incomplete. Its analytical model can score many mappings cheaply, yet changed layer shapes can make the winner irrelevant to deployment, and physical or verification checks may reject it later. Improving workload inputs or checking selected candidates can help more than accelerating an already inexpensive analytical step.

Likewise, a simulator run against an outdated workload or misconfigured memory model occupies a compute slot without answering the architecture question. Correcting those inputs increases useful evaluation throughput even when the simulator runs no faster. In another project, the inputs may be sound but every candidate allowed by the hardware template may miss the target. More runs then cannot supply a feasible design; the architect has to reconsider the organization or the requirements.

When viable proposals are flowing, evaluation and review capacity limit how much work can finish. A backlog grows at a stage whenever more work enters than completes over the same interval (@fig-scissors-gap). Candidate counts alone hide this imbalance because some candidates pass a quick check while others require long simulations or new verification effort.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The print-size workflow needs flexible placement beside the conditional backlog discussion. -->
![**Backlog depends on admitted work and completed checks.** This unscaled flow diagram separates proposal generation, admission, evaluation, and review. Waiting work grows at a stage when admissions exceed completions over the same interval. Admission and staged screening control how much generated work reaches the limited resources. The diagram specifies no measured rates or trend with architectural scope.](images/fig-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Unscaled flow diagram connecting proposal generation, admission, evaluation, and review to a completed decision. Waiting work is distinguished from completed checks; admission and screening determine which proposals enter the checking loop."}

The distinction between proposal generation and admission in @fig-scissors-gap gives the team a practical choice. It can improve screening so fewer unpromising candidates reach the scarce tools, add capacity at the limiting stage, or reduce work per check without weakening what the decision requires. A faster generator helps only if the added proposals improve the choices available enough to justify their downstream cost.

Cheaper generation can even increase total resource use if teams respond by submitting more work. The International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors and the joint Semiconductor Research Corporation and Semiconductor Industry Association Decadal Plan document the broader design productivity problem [@ITRS2001Design; @SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. Tools that make larger designs possible must be matched by ways to evaluate and check them.

::: {.callout-law title="The Jevons Paradox of Automated Generation"}
**The Classical Principle:** Greater efficiency can encourage increased consumption that outstrips the initial savings, a rebound effect Jevons documented for coal consumption [@Jevons1865CoalQuestion].

**The Hardware Trap:** When cheaper RTL generation leads a team to submit more candidates to simulation and physical implementation checks, demand for compute clusters and EDA licenses rises. The drafting saving remains real, yet the extra simulation, implementation, and review can outweigh it, so the complete study consumes more resources overall.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Decide how many candidates are worth running through slow simulators and verification tools and which checks each candidate needs, then measure total effort for the architectural result rather than the cost of producing one draft. Selective filtering and staged screening provide practical controls (@sec-law-jevons-paradox in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

### Matching Assistance to Limiting Work {#sec-where-ai-assistance-targets-design-pressures}

A bottleneck diagnosis becomes useful when it changes where the team invests. If a study cannot begin because a working RTL block or testbench is missing, a generator may reduce the preparation effort. If candidates already wait for simulation, a screening predictor or automated failure triage may be more useful. The same method can therefore accelerate one project and add delay to another.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Relieve the true limiting constraint"}
**The principle:** Target assistance at the work that actively delays the next design decision, whether missing inputs, candidate preparation, expensive evaluation, or expert review.

**The application:** Compare total effort and calendar delay before and after the change, including preparation, tool use, integration, and checking. Preserve the evidence the decision requires. Relieving one bottleneck can expose another, so repeat the diagnosis as the study progresses.
:::

Different forms of assistance address different missing work. The possibilities in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound pair a potential saving with the checks still needed to use the result. A draft can remove repetitive implementation work, for example, while leaving interface correctness and physical feasibility unresolved.

| **Limiting work** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What still establishes the result** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Context is scattered or stale | Reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information; flag missing details or stale assumptions. | Manual search across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and architectural judgment that the information is sufficient. |
| Strong evaluation is scarce | Estimate performance, power, physical risk, or uncertainty before a stronger tool is run. | High-fidelity evaluations spent on candidates unlikely to change design decisions. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design region, and checks on finalists. |
| A needed artifact is missing | Draft RTL, compiler code, tests, constraints, or candidate organizations. | Repetitive artifact creation and the initial pass through a design choice. | Interface rules, compilation or synthesis, verification, and physical checks appropriate to the artifact. |
| The choice space exceeds the budget | Search mappings, schedules, parameters, or topologies under stated objectives and constraints. | Manual sweeps and repeated selection among large numbers of choices. | A complete objective, legal choices, matched evaluation budgets, and stronger evaluation of the selected result. |
| Tool operation or triage consumes attention | Configure tools, launch runs, classify failures, compare reports, and route uncertain cases. | Repeated tool operation and initial result triage. | Clean tool state, reproducible commands, declared tool results, and expert review where required. |
: **Match assistance to the limiting work and retain the necessary checks.** Each row identifies a possible saving and the evidence needed to use its output in a design decision. {#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[22,28,24,26]"}

The scarce-evaluation row is useful when a calibrated predictor can avoid expensive runs that are unlikely to change the decision. It is less compelling when the existing analytical model already evaluates candidates cheaply. Similarly, a tool that gathers scattered context helps only if the returned information is accurate and sufficient; it cannot replace an unavailable foundry model or invent a missing workload trace.

Conventional automation remains a serious alternative. A regression pipeline can rerun benchmarks under a new compiler and flag changes in candidate rankings without using a learned model. Deterministic legality checks can discard impossible configurations before search. Learned methods may help interpret failures, rank candidates, or propose alternatives, but their setup and checking costs must fit the work they replace (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

Those costs include the expensive simulations used to train a surrogate, a learned model that predicts what a slower tool would report, verification of generated artifacts, and the compute, licenses, and review required by tool-using systems. Representative data may be unavailable, an independent check may be missing, or a conventional method may already solve the limiting task within budget. In those cases, the argument for adding AI is weak. When the requirements themselves are infeasible, reformulating the question or stopping the search is the appropriate outcome.

Point assistance can relieve a bounded task without organizing an entire study. An AI-native design system must additionally keep hardware choices, software paths, tool feedback, and checks coherent as the study changes. Whether that coordination improves the architecture result or reduces the total cost of obtaining it remains a comparison to be made, not a consequence of using more capable models.

\FloatBarrier

## Open Questions

The chapter identifies ways to locate limiting work, but it does not establish how reliably an automated system can choose which work to undertake next. The remaining questions concern the cost of obtaining useful evidence under physical, software, and verification constraints.

- **When a model can generate thousands of candidate designs a day, how do we decide which ones are worth running through slow simulators and verification tools?** Cheaper drafting can send more work into fixed checking capacity. Some candidates need only a short simulation; others require physical implementation and new verification effort. We still need reliable ways to weigh what a candidate may teach us against the work required to check it.

- **How can fast early models detect hidden physical bottlenecks outside a familiar hardware template?** Analytical models and learned predictors omit some wire, memory, and switching effects to remain inexpensive. A new organization can exploit those omissions and appear efficient until layout reveals extra traffic, congestion, or supply-voltage problems. The unresolved question is which cheap checks can warn of those failures early enough to guide exploration without reproducing the cost of detailed implementation.

- **Can we estimate how hard a candidate will be to verify before writing its RTL?** A cache-coherence shortcut or asynchronous interface can improve simulated performance while adding transient states, clock-domain interactions, and difficult proof obligations. Search tools need ways to anticipate that effort without treating verification as a fixed cost shared by all candidates. Such estimates must also distinguish a difficult but useful design from one whose checks merely need better decomposition or tooling.

- **How should architects weigh present efficiency against flexibility for future workloads?** Specializing a dataflow, scratchpad, or number format can improve efficiency while making the hardware sensitive to changed tensor shapes, memory behavior, and invocation sizes. Programmable units and flexible storage cost area and energy now, but may keep later workloads from losing their offload advantage. Co-design methods need to compare these costs under realistic uncertainty about workload and compiler change.

- **How can automated tools combine opaque IP and multi-vendor chiplets with adequate confidence in their interactions?** Interface standards expose part of a block's behavior while leaving internal queues, power states, and timing assumptions hidden. Individually verified blocks can still fail together under bursty traffic or incompatible reset sequences. Automated exploration needs enough interface information and probing to assess these interactions without requiring access to proprietary internal circuits.

## Summary

Architectural gains increasingly depend on how microarchitecture, specialization, software, and physical layout work together. The examples in this chapter make those couplings concrete: a faster arithmetic block can lose its advantage to offload overhead, a wider vector grouping can trigger register spills, and lower compute energy can be erased by off-chip memory traffic. Any useful comparison has to include the cross-layer interactions that can flip which design wins.

Exploring those trade-offs takes implementation effort, simulation time, and verification capacity. A large design space does not automatically make a study expensive, and an expensive study does not automatically call for AI. Where automation helps depends on which bottleneck is actually holding up the next engineering decision, what alternatives a tool makes practical to test, and what it costs to get an answer the team can trust. An AI-native design system must show that coordinating this work improves the result or reduces the total cost of reaching it. Coupled choices alone do not establish that benefit.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Follow the full cost of a local speedup.** Include data movement, control, software overhead, and physical layout effects before treating a block-level gain as a system gain.
- **Evaluate hardware together with its software.** Compiler mappings, runtime behavior, and workload shifts can change which hardware organization wins.
- **Pick the modeling boundary that answers the question.** Include the cross-layer interactions that can flip the decision, using the simplest abstraction that captures them at each scale.
- **Budget for evaluation and verification, not just generation.** Candidate counts, simulation runtime, verification effort, and engineering cost are distinct bottlenecks, and tests, surrogates, and formal proofs establish different things.
- **Aim assistance at the real bottleneck and measure the whole workflow.** Use the simplest method the problem needs, including conventional automation, and count setup, simulation, and review time alongside the task that became faster.
:::

Once a team knows which bottleneck is delaying its next decision, it needs a disciplined way to organize the study around that bottleneck. A simulator number has to stay tied to the exact workload and candidate it measured, and a failed check has to inform the next design step. Those obligations fit together across an explicit design life cycle that connects the initial architecture question to candidate generation, tool execution, evidence checks, and the final engineering decision (@sec-architecture-20-ontology).
